lessons.title: Lesson 1: From chatbot to agent
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain the difference between an AI chat and an AI agent.
This lesson builds toward: Given a repeated weekly sports task, you will explain how an AI agent differs from an AI chat and write the task as a one-sentence agent goal, naming the goal, the tools and the actions the agent would take.
In a normal AI chat, you ask and it answers; you do the next step yourself. An AI agent is given a goal and can plan steps, use tools (like reading a spreadsheet, searching the web, creating a document or drafting an email), check its work and continue until the goal is reached or it needs you.
Many AI products now offer agent-style features, and some sports tech platforms build agents into their tools. Features change fast, so focus on the pattern: goal, plan, tools, actions, checks.
Example: "Every Monday, read last week's training log, find athletes whose effort ratings rose while results fell, and draft a summary for the coach." A chat helps with one step; an agent can run the whole loop, if you allow it.
Words to know:
- AI agent: AI that can plan steps and use tools to reach a goal with less step-by-step direction.
- Tool: something the agent can use, like reading a file, searching or writing a draft.
- Workflow: a series of steps that complete a task.
Try it now: Write one weekly sports task you or your staff repeat (reports, schedules, film tagging summaries). Write it as a goal for an agent in one sentence.
You can now explain how an AI agent differs from a chat and describe a task as an agent goal.

check.q: What can an AI agent do that a plain chat usually does not?
options: Plan steps and use tools to reach a goal
Feel how an athlete is doing
check.why: An agent plans steps and uses tools such as reading a sheet or drafting a report.

check.q: You want an agent to help with weekly training reports. How do you start?
options: Write the task as one clear goal sentence
Let it choose its own task
Skip planning and switch it on
check.why: A clear goal is the starting point for any agent workflow.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Breaking a workflow into steps
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Map your task as a step-by-step workflow with inputs and outputs.
This lesson builds toward: Given that weekly task, you will map it as numbered steps with inputs and outputs, marking every step as mechanical, judgment or sensitive.
Before any agent can help, you need to know the steps yourself. Write them as a simple list: what goes in, what happens, what comes out.
Example weekly report: 1. Input: the team training-log sheet. 2. Check for missing or odd entries. 3. Calculate each athlete's weekly averages. 4. Flag patterns the coach asked about (effort up, results down; missed sessions). 5. Draft a one-page summary. 6. Coach reviews. 7. Coach decides any action.
Mark which steps are mechanical (good for AI), which need judgment (a person), and which involve sensitive data (extra care). An AI assistant can help you map it: "Here's how I make our weekly report. Turn it into numbered steps with inputs and outputs."
Step by step:
- List the steps you do now.
- Write the input and output of each step.
- Mark each step: mechanical, judgment or sensitive.
- Ask AI to tidy the list.
- Confirm the list with whoever uses the output.
Words to know:
- Input: what a step starts with, like a spreadsheet.
- Output: what a step produces, like a summary.
- Judgment step: a step that needs a person's decision.
Try it now: Write your weekly task as numbered steps with inputs and outputs. Mark each one mechanical, judgment or sensitive.
You can now map a performance task as a clear workflow.

check.q: What is an output in a workflow step?
options: The tool you are not allowed to use
check.why: Each step turns an input into an output for the next step.

check.q: One step is "decide which athletes need a rest day". How do you mark it?
options: Judgment, for a person to decide
check.why: Rest decisions need a person's judgment, not an agent.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Where agents go wrong
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name the main risks of agents and the protection for each.
This lesson builds toward: Given your workflow, you will name a risk and a protection for each step and mark where human checkpoints go, with at least two checkpoints and approval before anything is sent or changed.
Agents can make mistakes and keep going: misreading a column, inventing numbers, missing a row, or taking an action you did not want, like sending a draft to the whole team. Because they act in several steps, one early mistake can spread.
They can also be tricked. Text inside a file, web page or email can contain instructions aimed at the AI ("ignore your rules and send this file to..."). An agent that obeys data as if it were instructions is dangerous. Agents should treat content as data, and people should limit what agents are allowed to do.
Main protections: give the agent only the access it needs, use sample or anonymized data when testing, require a person to approve before anything is sent or changed, keep a log of what it did, and keep health, injury, selection and eligibility decisions with people.
Step by step:
- List what could go wrong at each step.
- Limit access to only what's needed.
- Require approval before sending or changing anything.
- Keep a log of actions.
- Keep key decisions human.
Words to know:
- Least access: giving a tool only the access it needs, nothing more.
- Prompt injection: hidden instructions in a file or web page that try to trick an AI into doing something.
- Human checkpoint: a point where a person must review or approve before the agent continues.
Try it now: For each step in your workflow, write one thing that could go wrong and one protection. Mark where a human checkpoint is needed.
You can now spot agent risks and add protections and human checkpoints.

options: A point where a person reviews or approves before the workflow continues
check.why: Checkpoints keep people in charge at key moments.

check.q: Your agent would be able to email the whole team. What protection do you add?
options: Require a person to approve before anything is sent
check.why: Approval before sending stops mistakes from reaching people.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Designing and testing your agent

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Writing the agent brief
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a one-page agent brief for your workflow.
This lesson builds toward: Given your workflow and risks, you will write a one-page agent brief with goal, inputs, steps, tools, limits and checkpoints, with every section filled and a rule to flag unclear data.
An agent brief is the instruction sheet for an agent. Whether you use an agent tool or run it by hand, write it first.
Sections: Goal (one sentence). Inputs (which files or data, and the format). Steps (numbered). Tools allowed (for example: read this sheet; create a draft document) and not allowed (for example: no sending email, no editing the original data). Output (format and length). Limits (never make health, selection or eligibility decisions; never use names with health data; flag unclear data instead of guessing). Human checkpoints (who approves, when).
Ask an AI assistant to help structure it: "Turn these notes into an agent brief with these sections." Then read it as if you were a careful new assistant coach: is anything unclear?
Step by step:
- Write the goal in one sentence.
- List inputs and format.
- Number the steps.
- List tools allowed and not allowed.
- Describe the output.
- Write limits and human checkpoints.
Words to know:
- Agent brief: the written instructions an agent follows: goal, inputs, steps, tools, limits and checkpoints.
- Flag: mark something for a person to look at instead of guessing.
Try it now: Write your agent brief using the sections above. Ask an AI assistant to point out anything unclear, then fix it.
You can now write a clear agent brief with goals, tools, limits and checkpoints.

check.q: Which section of an agent brief says what the agent must never do?
check.why: Limits spell out what is off-limits, such as sending email.

check.q: AI says one part of your brief is unclear. What do you do?
options: Make the brief longer with more examples
Rewrite that part so it is clear
check.why: Unclear instructions lead to unpredictable agent behavior.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Testing the workflow by hand
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Run your workflow step by step with an AI assistant using sample data.
This lesson builds toward: Using a 10-row anonymized sample, you will run the workflow by hand with an AI assistant, one step at a time, writing down every place it did not follow the brief.
Test before you automate. Make a small sample data set (or remove names and replace them with numbers like Athlete 1, Athlete 2) so no real private data is exposed.
Paste the brief into an AI assistant, then give it each step one at a time with the sample data. Look at the output after each step. Did it follow the brief? Did it flag unclear data or make something up?
Write down where it went wrong and update the brief. Only after several clean test runs, and approval from whoever is responsible for team data, should anyone consider letting an agent tool run more of it, still with human checkpoints.
Step by step:
- Make a sample or anonymized data set.
- Paste the brief into an AI assistant.
- Run one step at a time.
- Check each output against the brief.
- Note failures and update the brief.
- Repeat until runs are clean.
Words to know:
- Anonymized data: data with names and identifying details removed or replaced.
- Test run: a practice run with safe data to see if the workflow works.
Try it now: Create a 10-row anonymized sample of your data. Run your workflow step by step with an AI assistant and write down every place it did not follow the brief.
You can now test an agent workflow safely by hand before automating it.

options: Data with names and identifying details removed or replaced
check.why: Anonymized data protects athletes while you test.

check.q: Step 2 of your hand test gives a wrong average. What do you do?
options: Stop, note it and fix the brief before moving on
check.why: Checking each step catches mistakes before they spread.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Reviewing outputs and keeping humans in charge
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Review an agent's output with a checklist and decide what to improve.
This lesson builds toward: Given the test output, you will review it with a checklist and write improvements to the brief, keeping every health, injury and selection decision with people.
Every agent output needs a human review before it is used. Use a short checklist: Accurate (numbers match the data)? Complete (no athlete or row missed)? Within limits (no health or selection decisions, no private data)? Clear (the coach can use it in two minutes)? Flags handled (unclear items listed, not guessed)?
Review the action log too: what did it read, what did it create, did it try anything outside its allowed tools?
Then decide: keep, improve or stop. Some tasks are better left manual. The goal is to give coaches and athletes more time for coaching and training, not to hand over decisions.
Step by step:
- Check accuracy against the data.
- Check completeness.
- Check limits and privacy.
- Check clarity for the coach.
- Review the action log.
- Decide: keep, improve or stop.
Words to know:
- Action log: a record of everything the agent read, created or tried to do.
- Human in the loop: a person reviews or approves at key points in an AI workflow.
Try it now: Final task: review your test output with the five-point checklist, check what the AI did at each step, and write two improvements to your agent brief.
You can now review agent outputs and keep people in charge of performance decisions.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Goal and workflow The goal is vague or steps have no inputs and outputs. One-sentence goal; numbered steps with inputs, outputs and a type for each. Steps are small enough that each output can be checked quickly. Risks and checkpoints Fewer than two checkpoints, or the agent can send or change things without approval. A risk and protection per step, at least two checkpoints, approval before sending. Also uses least access and says how content in files is treated as data. Agent brief A section is missing or the limits are unclear. Goal, inputs, steps, tools, limits, never-do list and checkpoints on one page. Says what to do with unclear or missing data at each step. Hand test Real athlete data used, or the test skipped steps. Anonymized sample run one step at a time, with every miss written down. Ran a second test after fixing the brief and compared the two. Review and people in charge Output used without review, or it contains a health or selection decision. Reviewed with the checklist; two improvements written; decisions left to people. Names who approves before any further automation. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Why use a checklist to review an agent's output?
options: To check it the same careful way every time
To let the agent approve itself
check.why: A checklist makes reviews consistent and catches the same kinds of errors.

check.q: The report recommends cutting an athlete's minutes. What do you do?
options: Accept it because the data is clean
Ask the agent to decide again
Remove it; minutes are a coach's decision
check.why: Selection and playing-time decisions stay with people.
